onboarding.title: What would you like help with?

options.label: Spend less time on feeds I regret
Make your workdays clearer and test where you can grow.
Learn by making small, real things you can test yourself.

onboarding.sub: Whatever actually gets you. No judgment.

onboarding.sub: Your honest average, not the best or worst day.

onboarding.title: What do you want more of?
How do you usually use AI tools?

onboarding.sub: Only pick ones you'd actually do.

onboarding.title: What kind of coach would help you most?

onboarding.title: How much effort do you want logging to take?

options.label: 30 seconds, a tap and a feeling

challenges.title: The One-Item Landing Pad
challenges.sub: Create one safe place for one object that keeps floating around.
challenges.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: a person sets their keys down into a small catch-all dish beside a wallet on an entryway table.

teach.title: One item is enough 🧺
lines: Clutter can feel loud because every object asks a question.
Where does this go? Do I need it? Can I deal with it later?
Today, we only answer one question — for one item.
teach.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: a person holds up a single set of keys while other objects sit blurred behind them.

teach.title: Give it a tiny home 🏠
lines: A landing pad is a temporary home.
It does not need to be perfect.
It just gives one object a place to rest, so your brain can stop tracking it.
teach.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: a small catch-all dish on a shelf with keys nestled inside, like a tiny home.

challenges.q: What object keeps showing up in the wrong place?

action.title: Try this now ✨
lines: Pick one object.
Choose one tiny landing pad.
Move the object there.
That is the whole challenge. No sorting, no cleaning spree — one object, one place.
action.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: a hand lowers a single pair of earbuds into a small dish on a table.

done.title: You lowered the mental noise today!
lines: You gave one thing a place to land.
That counts.

challenges.title: The Visible Surface Reset
challenges.sub: Clear one small surface you can actually see.
challenges.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: a person wipes clean one small patch on an otherwise lightly cluttered desk.

teach.title: You do not need the whole room 🪄
lines: Your brain can feel relief from one visible patch of progress.
Not the whole desk. Not the whole kitchen.
Just one small surface you can look at and say: that part changed.
teach.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: a lightly cluttered desk with one small clean cleared square standing out as tidy.

teach.title: Make the win obvious 👀
lines: A visible reset works because your eyes can find the win again later.
It becomes proof that motion happened.
Even if the rest is still messy.
teach.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: a person glances with a satisfied smile at one clean cleared patch on their desk.

challenges.q: Which tiny surface feels easiest today?

action.title: Clear one small patch 🧽
lines: Pick a surface.
Clear a space about the size of a book.
Move anything that does not belong out of that patch.
Stop when the patch is visible.
action.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: a hand wipes clean one small book-sized square on a cluttered desk with a cloth.

done.title: You made progress you can see!
lines: One visible spot is not nothing.
It is a signal to your brain: I can start small and still change the room.

challenges.title: The Trash-Only Sweep
challenges.sub: Remove only obvious trash, so your brain has fewer decisions to make.
challenges.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: a person drops an empty cup into a trash bag in a tidy living room.

teach.title: Decisions are the heavy part 🧠
lines: Cleaning often gets stuck because every item becomes a decision.
Keep it? Move it? Donate it?
Not today. Today, we only look for obvious trash.
teach.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: a person pauses thoughtfully, hand near chin, considering a few scattered items around the room.

teach.title: Trash has a clear next step 🗑️
lines: Obvious trash is easier because it already has a destination.
Wrapper. Empty cup. Old receipt. Packaging.
If you have to debate it, skip it.
teach.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: a small grouping of obvious trash on a surface — a crumpled wrapper, empty cup, and cardboard.

challenges.q: What kind of trash feels easiest to remove first?

opts.l: The first obvious thing I see

action.title: Do a trash-only sweep ✨
lines: Grab a bag or bin.
Pick up only obvious trash.
Skip anything that makes you think too hard.
When the timer ends, stop.
action.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: a person walks through the room with an open trash bag, reaching to pick up a crumpled wrapper.

done.title: You made the space lighter!
lines: You removed decisions from the room.
That is real progress.

challenges.title: The Phone-Free First Coffee
challenges.sub: Drink one warm drink with your phone waiting somewhere else.
challenges.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: a person cradles a warm mug with eyes closed while their phone lies face-down and away on the counter.

teach.title: The first input sets the pace ☀️
lines: The first thing you give your attention often sets its speed for hours.
A feed teaches it to sprint.
A warm drink teaches it to sit still.
teach.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: a warm mug with rising steam on a sunny windowsill in soft golden morning light.

teach.title: Notice the reach 🫖
lines: The urge to reach for a phone can change when you give it a little room.
What is left is just a quiet morning.
Notice how it feels to keep this small part of the morning to yourself.
teach.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: a person pulls their hand back from a face-down phone and reaches for a warm mug instead.

challenges.q: Where will your phone wait?

action.title: Make the drink, park the phone ✨
lines: Put the phone in its waiting spot.
Make your drink.
Drink it looking at anything that is not a screen.
If your hand wanders, just notice it. That counts as data.
action.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: a person sets their phone on a far shelf while a warm mug waits on the counter.

done.title: You gave your attention a slow start!
lines: Ninety seconds of itch, then a quiet morning.
Noted.

challenges.title: Ten Minutes, One Thing
challenges.sub: Give one task your whole attention for ten minutes, and notice what pulls you away.

teach.title: Switching has a cost 🔀
lines: Each time you jump between tasks, part of your mind stays behind.
Ten tabs open can feel like ten small voices talking at once.
One thing at a time is not slower. It is often quieter.

teach.title: The pull is the lesson 🧲
lines: You will probably feel tugs toward other things. That is normal.
You do not have to fight them. Just notice them and come back.
Every return is the practice working, not failing.

challenges.q: What one thing will get your ten minutes?

opts.l: One email I keep putting off
Reading one thing all the way
Whatever is right in front of me

action.title: One thing, ten minutes 🎯
lines: Close or hide everything that is not this one thing.
Start the timer and begin anywhere.
When a tug pulls you elsewhere, notice it and come back. Standing, pacing, or fidgeting is fine.
When the timer ends, stop, even mid-sentence.

done.title: You stayed with one thing.
lines: However many times you wandered, you came back each time.
That returning is a real skill, and you just used it.

challenges.title: The Five-Sound Walk
challenges.sub: Take a short walk without your phone and listen for five distinct sounds.

teach.title: Ears go first 👂
lines: Most of us walk through the world looking, and half-planning the next thing.
Listening pulls you into the present in a different way.
Sounds only happen now. You cannot listen to yesterday.

teach.title: Small sounds count 🍃
lines: A bird is a sound. So is a fridge hum, a car door, or your own footsteps.
You are not looking for beautiful sounds. Just real ones.
If you only find three, that is still a walk well spent.

challenges.q: Where can you walk for a few minutes?

opts.l: A parking lot or quiet street

action.title: Walk and listen 🚶
lines: Leave your phone behind, or put it deep in a bag.
Walk at any pace that feels easy.
Count five distinct sounds on your fingers as you hear them.
Before you head back, stand still for a few breaths and listen once more.

done.title: You heard the world for a while.
lines: Those sounds were there all along.
Now you know how to find them again.

challenges.title: The Done List
challenges.sub: Write down what you already did today, instead of what you still have to do.

teach.title: To-do lists only look forward 🔭
lines: A to-do list is always longer than the day.
It quietly tells you that you are behind, no matter what you finish.
A done list tells the other half of the story.

teach.title: Invisible work is still work 🫙
lines: Answering a hard text, feeding someone, getting out of bed on a heavy day.
None of it shows up on a to-do list, and all of it took effort.
Writing it down makes the effort visible, even just to you.

challenges.q: What kind of day has it been so far?

opts.l: Busy, but it feels like nothing got done

action.title: Write what is already done ✍️
lines: Grab paper or a notes app.
List everything you did today, starting from waking up.
Include the small and invisible things. They count.
Read the list once, slowly, before you close it.

done.title: Look how much was already there.
lines: The day held more than the to-do list could see.
You were moving all along.

challenges.title: The No-Agenda Hello
challenges.sub: Send one person a short message that asks nothing of them.

teach.title: Most messages want something 📨
lines: Can you, did you, when will, just checking.
Even friendly messages often carry a small request.
A message that asks for nothing feels different to receive.

teach.title: Small is the point 🌱
lines: It does not need to be deep or clever.
"Saw a dog that looked like yours and thought of you" is plenty.
If they do not reply, the message still did its work.

challenges.q: Who comes to mind first?

opts.l: A friend I have not talked to in a while
Someone I keep meaning to reach

action.title: Say hello, ask nothing 👋
lines: Pick one person.
Write one or two sentences that share a thought, a memory, or simple warmth.
Read it once and remove any question that asks them to do something.
Send it, then let it go.

done.title: Someone got a light message today.
lines: You offered warmth without a hook attached.
Whatever comes back, the gift is already given.

challenges.title: Two Readings of One Irritation
challenges.sub: Take one recent annoyance and find a second, equally plausible story about it.

teach.title: The first story arrives fast ⚡
lines: When something irritates you, your mind writes a story in a split second.
They are careless. They do not respect me. This always happens.
The story feels like a fact because it came so quickly.

teach.title: A second reading is not an excuse 📖
lines: Finding another explanation does not mean the first one is wrong.
It means you can choose your response with more of the picture.
Sometimes the second reading changes nothing. Sometimes it changes everything.

challenges.q: Where did the irritation come from?

opts.l: A stranger, like in traffic or a line
Something I read or saw online

action.title: Read it twice 🔍
lines: Write one sentence about what happened, just the facts a camera would see.
Write your first reading: the story you told yourself.
Write a second reading that would also fit the facts.
Ask: if the second one were true, what would I do differently? Pick one small, proportionate response, or none.
Note one thing to watch for next time to learn which reading was closer.

done.title: You held two stories at once.
lines: That small gap between the facts and your first story is where choice lives.
You found it today.

challenges.title: The Fear Under the Avoided Task
challenges.sub: Look honestly at one task you keep avoiding and name what it is really asking of you.

teach.title: Avoidance is information 🧭
lines: A task you keep skipping is rarely just boring.
Often it touches something tender: being judged, being wrong, or being done with something.
Avoidance is not a character flaw. It is a signal worth reading.

teach.title: Name it to shrink it 🔦
lines: A vague dread is huge. A named fear has edges.
"I am afraid the number will be bad" is easier to hold than a cloud of not-wanting.
Once it has edges, you can find one small first step around it.

challenges.q: What kind of task have you been avoiding?

opts.l: A creative project I care about

action.title: Find the real weight 🪨
lines: Write the task at the top of a page.
Finish this sentence three times: "If I do this, I might have to..."
Circle the line that makes your stomach tighten. That is the real weight.
Write one step so small it does not touch that weight yet, like opening the folder. Do it now if you can.

done.title: You looked at the thing behind the thing.
lines: Naming a fear takes more courage than doing a chore.
The task is the same size. You know it better now.

challenges.title: A Values Audit of One Week
challenges.sub: Compare what you say matters with where last week's hours actually went.

teach.title: Time tells the truth gently 🕰️
lines: Most of us carry a list of what matters: people, health, a craft, faith, rest.
A calendar shows where the hours really went.
The gap between the two is not a verdict. It is a map.

teach.title: Some gaps are chosen 🤲
lines: A week caring for a sick parent may leave no room for a hobby, and that is a value too.
The question is not "Did I fail?" but "Did I choose this?"
Look for the hours that went somewhere you did not choose.

challenges.q: How did last week feel, looking back?

opts.l: Swept along by other people's needs

action.title: Lay the two side by side 🗓️
lines: Write three things you say matter most to you right now.
Look at last week through your calendar, messages, or memory. Note roughly where the hours went.
Mark where the week matched your three, and one place it drifted without your choosing.
Pick one hour next week to give back to something on your list. Just one.

done.title: You saw your week honestly.
lines: Not to judge it, just to know it.
One reclaimed hour is a real change of direction.

challenges.title: The Pattern Behind the Pile
challenges.sub: Look at one pile that keeps coming back and find the decision it is waiting for.

teach.title: Piles are paused decisions ⏸️
lines: A pile is rarely about laziness.
It usually holds items that each need a decision you are not ready to make.
Clearing it once does not help much if the same decision keeps getting skipped.

teach.title: Look for the repeat 🔁
lines: If the same kind of thing keeps landing there, that is a pattern.
Mail you do not want to open. Clothes worn once. Projects half begun.
Find the pattern and you can change the system, not just the pile.

challenges.q: Which pile keeps coming back?

opts.l: A digital pile, like downloads or tabs

action.title: Read the pile 🧩
lines: Pick up five items from the pile, one at a time.
For each, say out loud what decision it is waiting for.
Notice which decision repeats. That is the pattern.
Make one small change for that decision only, like a bin for worn-once clothes. Leave the rest of the pile for another day.

done.title: You found what the pile was saying.
lines: The pile may still be there.
But now it has one less reason to grow.

challenges.title: A Repair Without a Request
challenges.sub: Draft an honest acknowledgment of your part in something, without asking to be forgiven.

teach.title: Asking for forgiveness asks for work 🎁
lines: "I'm sorry, can you forgive me?" quietly hands the other person a job.
They now have to reassure you, sometimes before they are ready.
A cleaner repair names your part and leaves them free.

teach.title: Your part, not the whole story 🧵
lines: You do not have to take all the blame to own your share.
Skip "but" and skip explaining their part.
If the hurt runs deep, it is okay to get support from someone you trust before you send anything.

challenges.q: What kind of moment needs repair?

opts.l: Something I let slide or forgot
A promise I did not keep
Not sure, just a lingering weight

action.title: Draft the repair 🪡
lines: Write what happened in one plain sentence, from your side only.
Name the likely effect on them, without guessing too much about their feelings.
Say what you will do differently, if you know. End there, with no request.
Read it back and remove any "but" or explanation. Send it now, later, or not at all. The draft is the challenge.

done.title: You owned your part cleanly.
lines: Whether you send it or not, you now see the moment more honestly.
Watch, over the next days, for how it sits with you.

challenges.title: A Boundary, Said Kindly
challenges.sub: Find the words for one limit you need, clear enough to hold and warm enough to say.

teach.title: A boundary is about you 🧱
lines: A boundary is not a rule for someone else's behavior.
It is a statement about what you will do.
"I'm not able to take calls after nine" lands differently than "You need to stop calling."

teach.title: Kind and clear can live together 🤝
lines: Many people soften a limit until it disappears.
Others harden it until it sounds like an attack.
The middle is warm about the person and firm about the line.

challenges.q: Where do you most need a limit right now?

opts.l: A topic I do not want to discuss

action.title: Find the words 🚧
lines: Write the limit as something you will or will not do.
Add one warm line about the person or the relationship.
Read it aloud. If it sounds cold, warm it. If it sounds vague, sharpen it.
Decide when you might say it, and what you will do if it is not respected.

done.title: You found the words for a line.
lines: Saying it may still feel hard, and that is normal.
You know what you mean now, and that makes it easier to say.

challenges.title: Let a Neighbor Choose
challenges.sub: Offer a little time to someone nearby and let them name the need.

teach.title: Guessing can miss 🎯
lines: We often help with what we would want, or what we are good at.
The other person may need something else entirely.
Letting them choose turns help into respect.

teach.title: Easy to decline matters 🕊️
lines: An offer that is hard to refuse can feel like pressure.
Give a clear window and a clear way out.
A "no thanks" still means the door is open.

challenges.q: Who nearby might welcome a hand?

opts.l: Someone going through a hard stretch
Anyone, I am not sure who yet

action.title: Make the offer 🏘️
lines: Pick one person and one window of time you could truly give.
Write a short offer: when you are free, that they choose what would help, and that no is fine.
Send it, knock, or leave a note.
If they say yes, do exactly what they ask, not what you planned.

done.title: You made room for someone else's need.
lines: Whatever they say, the offer itself says you notice them.
That is how neighborhoods get knit together.

challenges.title: The Specific Thank-You
challenges.sub: Thank someone whose quiet work makes your life easier, and name exactly what it made possible.

teach.title: Thanks gets lost in general 🌫️
lines: "Thanks for everything" is kind, but it slides right off.
"Because you fixed that schedule, I made it to my kid's game" sticks.
Specific thanks shows someone that their work reached a real life.

teach.title: Look for the invisible helpers 🔦
lines: The coworker who cleans up the shared file. The person who runs the food pantry.
A teacher, a bus driver, a neighbor who shovels the walk.
These people rarely hear what their work made possible.

challenges.q: Whose quiet work do you rely on?

opts.l: A coworker who keeps things running
Someone whose name I do not even know

action.title: Write the thank-you 💌
lines: Name the person and one specific thing they did.
Write what that thing made possible for you, in one concrete sentence.
Keep it short. Skip asking for anything back.
Send it, hand it over, or say it in person. A note on paper counts.

done.title: Someone's quiet work was seen today.
lines: You showed them where their effort landed.
That kind of seeing helps hold a community together.

challenges.title: Fifteen Quiet Minutes
challenges.sub: Sit, walk, or kneel in silence for fifteen minutes with one simple anchor.

teach.title: Silence is not empty 🌌
lines: Many traditions, religious and not, keep a practice of silence.
Not to stop thinking, but to see thoughts arrive and pass.
In the quiet, what matters tends to rise to the surface.

teach.title: Choose an anchor that fits you ⚓
lines: A short prayer, a line of a poem, a single word, or simply the breath.
When your mind wanders, and it will, gently return to the anchor.
You can move, sway, or walk slowly. Still does not have to mean motionless.

challenges.q: What anchor feels right today?

opts.l: A line of poetry or scripture

action.title: Enter the quiet 🕯️
lines: Put your phone face down after starting the timer.
Settle into a position you can hold comfortably, or begin a slow walk.
Bring your anchor to mind. When thoughts pull you away, notice them and come back.
When the timer ends, sit for one more breath before you move on.

done.title: You kept fifteen minutes of quiet.
lines: Whatever rose up or wandered off, you stayed and returned.
That is the whole practice.

challenges.title: A Five-Line Rule of Life
challenges.sub: Write five short lines that describe how you want to live, in your own words.

teach.title: An old idea, made small 🏛️
lines: Monastic communities have long kept a "rule of life": a short guide to how they live.
It was never meant as a cage. It was more like a trellis for growth.
Yours can be five lines, written for no one but you.

teach.title: Describe, do not demand 🌿
lines: "I begin the day slowly" holds better than "I must wake at five."
Write lines you could return to after a hard week, not ones that scold you.
A good rule helps you come back. It does not keep score.

challenges.q: What do you most want your days to hold?

action.title: Write your rule 📜
lines: Write five lines, each beginning with "I" and describing a way of living, not a goal.
Try one each for body, mind, people, work, and spirit, or any five that feel true.
Read them aloud. Cross out any line that sounds like a should.
Keep the page somewhere you will see it again.

done.title: You wrote down how you want to live.
lines: It can change. Rules of life are meant to be revised.
For now, you have something to come home to.

challenges.title: Pass One Thing On
challenges.sub: Choose one thing life has taught you, and prepare to share it with someone who could use it.

teach.title: What you know was given to you 🎁
lines: Most of what you know came from someone: a parent, a coach, a book, a hard year.
Passing it on closes the circle.
It does not have to be wisdom. A practical skill counts just as much.

teach.title: Teach from where you stand 🪜
lines: You do not need to be an expert.
The best teacher is often one step ahead and still remembers being stuck.
Share the thing, and share how you learned it.

challenges.q: What kind of thing could you pass on?

opts.l: A practical skill, like cooking or fixing
A way of thinking that helped me
Something a hard time taught me
A book, idea, or practice I love

action.title: Prepare to pass it on 🎓
lines: Name the one thing and the person who could use it.
Write how you learned it, in three or four sentences, including where you got stuck.
Boil it down to one thing they could try this week.
Share it now, or set a time to share it. Ask afterward what was useful.

done.title: Something you carry can now travel.
lines: Someone gave it to you once, and now you are giving it onward.
That is how knowing stays alive.

challenges.title: A Letter About What to Keep
challenges.sub: Write to your future self about what you have learned is worth holding on to.

teach.title: Change makes us forget 🌊
lines: In a year, your life may look quite different.
Busy seasons have a way of washing out what you learned in quieter ones.
A letter can carry it across.

teach.title: Keep, not fix 🫶
lines: This is not a letter of goals or corrections.
It is a note about what is already good and true, and worth protecting.
Write as a friend who knows you well and wants you to remember.

challenges.q: What feels most worth keeping right now?

opts.l: Certain people and how we are together
A habit or practice that steadies me
A way of seeing things I learned
Something about who I am becoming

action.title: Write the letter ✉️
lines: Start with "Dear me, a year from now."
Name three things worth keeping, and why each one matters.
Add one gentle reminder for a day when things feel hard.
Seal it, schedule it, or tuck it away somewhere you will find it.

done.title: You sent something forward.
lines: Your future self will meet this version of you again.
What you chose to keep says a lot about who you are.

energyMessages.empty: Noted. Gentle mode — tiny wins only today.
energyMessages.mid: Steady. A normal-sized day it is.

items: Vacuum or sweep the whole home

daily.title: Daily reset
daily.sub: The little things that keep chaos away.

rooms.title: Kitchen
items: Put away items on the counter
Clean up spills in the fridge
Take out trash & replace the bag

rooms.title: Bathroom
items: Put out clean towels & restock soap

rooms.title: Bedroom
items: Put dirty clothes in the hamper

maintenance.title: Put out clean kitchen towels
maintenance.tip: Swap out damp or soiled towels and hang the fresh ones where they can dry.

maintenance.title: Check the range hood filter
maintenance.tip: Use the hood manual to check whether its filter should be washed or replaced.

maintenance.title: Swap bathroom towels
maintenance.tip: Put out fresh towels and give them room to air-dry between uses.

maintenance.title: Dust the exhaust fan cover
maintenance.tip: Switch the fan off and wipe accessible dust from the outside of the cover.

maintenance.title: Check whether the mattress needs rotating
maintenance.tip: Follow the maker’s instructions. Ask for help moving a heavy mattress.

maintenance.title: Clear and vacuum under the bed
maintenance.tip: Pull out one bin or box at a time to make the floor reachable.

maintenance.title: Clear the air vents
maintenance.tip: Move furniture or baskets away from grilles and dust their accessible surfaces.

maintenance.title: Check the upholstery care tags
maintenance.tip: Find the care instructions before washing removable covers or treating a stain.

maintenance.title: Check your last backup
maintenance.tip: Open your backup tool and confirm a recent backup completed.

maintenance.title: Clear dust around device vents
maintenance.tip: Power off devices first and follow each manufacturer’s cleaning instructions.

maintenance.title: Inspect extension cords
maintenance.tip: Set aside cords with damaged insulation, loose plugs, or scorch marks.

maintenance.title: Look for leaks around stored equipment
maintenance.tip: Check for drips or pooling and identify where they came from before cleanup.

maintenance.title: Check the heating and AC filter
maintenance.tip: Check the filter size and system manual. Clean a reusable filter or replace a dirty disposable filter as directed.

maintenance.title: Check water softener salt
maintenance.tip: If you have a salt-based softener, check the brine tank and top it up with the salt specified in its manual.

maintenance.title: Look for leaks by the water heater
maintenance.tip: Look for drips or pooling around the unit. Have a qualified professional inspect any leak.

maintenance.title: Clear the main path through your home
maintenance.tip: Move shoes, bags and cords away from doorways and the path you use most.

maintenance.title: Look for damp spots under the sink
maintenance.cadence: Before a busy week or trip
maintenance.tip: Look for drips, damp cabinet flooring or water stains without adjusting fittings. If you find moisture, tell building maintenance or a plumber.

maintenance.title: Test your smoke alarms
maintenance.tip: Use the test control according to the manufacturer’s instructions. If an alarm doesn’t respond, follow the manual or contact building maintenance.

maintenance.title: Look over any decorative lights you’ll use
maintenance.tip: Set aside strands with damaged cords or broken sockets. Follow the product instructions for connecting strands.

seasonal.title: Holiday season
seasonal.summary: Pick what helps, whether you’re celebrating, working, traveling, keeping things quiet, or just getting through it.

tips.title: Two things can be true
tips.summary: Give mixed feelings a little room.
tips.body:
Try putting two things you feel into one sentence with “and.” You might miss someone and look forward to a quiet meal. You might enjoy seeing people and be relieved when you get home.

Both feelings belong. Think of one small thing that would make the next hour a little easier.

tips.title: Take a minute before you go in
tips.summary: Give yourself a pause before a visit, call, or shift.
tips.body:
Before you open the door, join the call, or start your shift, give yourself a moment. Ask what you want to keep some room for in the next hour. It could be privacy, patience, or enough energy to get home.

Choose one way to protect it. You can keep an answer brief, take a break, or head home when you said you would.

tips.title: Make room for what you miss
tips.summary: A small way to acknowledge an absence or a change.
tips.body:
If you’re missing a person, place, or part of your life, choose a small acknowledgment that feels right today. Put on a song you associate with them, walk somewhere familiar, or write a sentence about the memory.

If a tradition feels too heavy this year, you can change it, share it with someone, or skip it.

checklists.title: Protect your time and budget
checklists.summary: Decide what fits before the weeks fill up.

items.title: Protect one evening or hour
items.detail: Put the time on your calendar before the week fills up.

items.title: Pick a spending limit you can live with
items.detail: Look at essentials first. If you have room for extras, include travel, meals and any gifts. Zero is a valid choice.

items.title: Keep one short reply ready
items.detail: Try “I’m keeping that week quiet, so I’ll pass. Thanks for thinking of me.”

items.title: Check one deadline that affects you
items.detail: Look up a return window, renewal date or bill in the original receipt or account. Put the date somewhere you’ll see it.

items.title: Mute one source of shopping pressure
items.detail: Pause one store’s notifications or unsubscribe from a sale email you tend to open.

checklists.title: When routines change
checklists.summary: Prepare for travel, guests, or a different week at home.

items.title: Check hours for two places you count on
items.detail: Check the posted hours for your grocery store, transit route, or another essential service.

items.title: Confirm the details that affect other people
items.detail: If you’re traveling or meeting someone, confirm timing and transport. If people are coming over, ask what would make the space easier to use.

items.title: Make one backup plan
items.detail: At home, set aside an easy meal. If you’ll be away, confirm who is covering pets, plants or packages.

items.title: Give essentials one place to land
items.detail: Put keys, chargers and anything you’ll need on the way out in the same spot.

items.title: Leave a gap afterward
items.detail: Keep a small stretch of time open after travel, a visit or a long shift, if you can.

checklists.title: A gentler day
checklists.summary: Make a hard, busy, or quiet day easier to get through.

items.title: Keep one ordinary thing
items.detail: Make the coffee you like, take your usual walk, read for a few minutes, or sit somewhere comfortable.

items.title: Make one demand smaller
items.detail: Choose an easier meal, shorten a visit, or move an errand to another day.

items.title: Reach out in a way that feels manageable
items.detail: If you want company, send someone a short text or ask if they have ten minutes to talk.

items.title: Take a break you’ll actually get
items.detail: Pause between calls, step outside, or sit somewhere quiet for a few minutes.

items.title: Leave one note for tomorrow
items.detail: Write down a single next step, then let the rest wait.

quotes.author: Glimmer

quotes.text: Give the person behind the desk the same patience you’d give a friend.
quotes.author: Glimmer

quotes.text: The trail you love is worth a morning with the cleanup crew.
quotes.author: Glimmer

quotes.text: Some rules outlast their purpose. Look at who has to do more work to keep them going.
quotes.author: Glimmer

coach.title: Mute or block one repeat rage-bait account
coach.sub: Keep your attention for people and ideas you value. Skip the argument and leave the feed.

coach.title: Make your feed reflect your interests
coach.sub: Review five accounts. Keep useful, constructive, and enjoyable sources; remove what repeatedly drains you.

coach.title: Mark one unwanted recommendation as Not interested
coach.sub: Use the nearest equivalent in your app, then stop browsing. Recommendations may take time to change.

coach.title: Trade one scroll session for five minutes of something you care about
coach.sub: Make something, move, contact someone, or rest. Notice how you feel afterward.

coach.title: Message a person instead of checking the feed
coach.sub: Ask a genuine question or share something specific. Online friendships count too.

coach.title: Take one break with the feed closed
coach.sub: Listen to a song, look outside, or sit comfortably. The break does not have to be productive.

short_video.title: Trade one short-video session for five minutes of something you care about
short_video.sub: Choose something enjoyable or restful, then log how it leaves you feeling.

ai_quiz.title: Ask AI to quiz you instead of summarizing for you
ai_quiz.sub: Turn one lookup into something that actually sticks.

change_of_scene.title: Swap one scroll session for a change of scene
change_of_scene.sub: Try a short walk, change seats, or look out a window. Notice how it feels.

contact_someone.title: Text one person something specific and real
contact_someone.sub: See how it feels compared with opening the feed.

notice_feed.title: Name how you feel before you open social media
notice_feed.sub: One word, in your head. That's the whole thing.

screen_free_meal.title: Try one phone-free meal
screen_free_meal.sub: Low stakes. Just notice what it feels like.

exercises.title: See if your manager teaches you
exercises.sub: Bring a specific project to your manager and ask what they would do differently next time. Afterward, note whether their answer gives you a concrete skill to practice.

exercises.title: Interview a prospective manager
exercises.sub: In an interview, ask a prospective manager to tell you about one person they helped grow. Notice how specific their story is, and use that answer to weigh whether the fit feels right.

exercises.title: Build one sample for a role you want
exercises.sub: Identify one skill in a role you want and build a tiny finished example of it this week. When you wrap up, note what felt natural and which part needs more practice.

exercises.title: Make the next ask smaller
exercises.sub: An unanswered message can mean all sorts of things. If you still want help, try one question that’s easy to answer. Instead of asking for career advice, you might ask someone which piece of your work they’d show first.

exercises.title: Find the pattern in your stuck moments
exercises.sub: Each workday, jot one line about where you stalled and what happened just before. On day seven, look for the repeat and name one condition you could change, not a flaw to fix.

exercises.title: Ease one handoff for someone else
exercises.sub: Choose one place where your work lands on someone else's desk. Each day, try one small change that makes it easier on their end. Midweek, ask them plainly whether it helped.

exercises.title: Make a tiny robot or circuit
exercises.sub: Use parts you own or an inexpensive beginner breadboard kit to light a battery-powered LED with its supplied resistor, then add a switch. Predict the result, test it, and diagnose any loose connection. Technology becomes understandable when you work with it hands-on.

exercises.title: Build a game, then play it
exercises.sub: Build a simple one-rule video game using a small maze or a single coin to collect. Play your own game first to feel how it works. Then change one rule, such as the speed or goal, and replay to notice how the experience shifts.

exercises.title: Try making a game mod
exercises.sub: Open the official editor or tutorial from a game you already own. Change one level or a single object, then run it to test how it plays. Trying out your own edit is a practical way to learn level design.

exercises.title: Try an AI agent on one small task
exercises.sub: Give an AI agent one small task you can check yourself, using only public or nonsensitive inputs. Review the result and note where it helped and where your own judgment mattered.

exercises.title: Run a service in Docker or Linux
exercises.sub: Choose one tool from its official source and run it locally on a computer you own. Keep it off the public internet. Write down one thing you learned about how it runs.

exercises.title: Make one rough thing
exercises.sub: Set a ten-minute timer and start something small, like a beat or sketch. Keep going without editing until time is up.

exercises.title: Learn one thing together
exercises.sub: Think of something you and a friend are both curious about. Ask if they’d like to try it with you. You could mend a seam together, taking turns with the needle. Neither of you has to be the expert.

exercises.title: Explain it to find the gap
exercises.sub: Each day, explain one thing you are learning out loud or on paper, as if to a curious friend. Mark the moment you start hand-waving. That spot is tomorrow's practice.

exercises.title: Write one beginner step a day
exercises.sub: Pick a hands-on skill you have. Each day, write or show one beginner step clearly enough to follow without you. By day seven you have a small guide you can pass on.

exercises.title: Watch one chosen show, guilt-free
exercises.sub: Name one show you genuinely want to watch tonight instead of slipping into automatic scrolling, and enjoy it guilt-free. Afterward, notice how a chosen break feels compared to drifting through a feed.

exercises.title: Choose your next gaming break
exercises.sub: Games can teach real skills and tell great stories, and both games and TV offer a welcome escape. Before you start, set a specific stopping point so you can enjoy the break and still keep time for something else you value.

exercises.title: Sort what restores from what passes
exercises.sub: Each evening, note one thing that left you more rested and one that only passed the time. No judgment, just sorting. By day seven, protect one restoring thing on purpose.

exercises.title: Say your rest out loud
exercises.sub: Each day, tell one person when you are stepping away and when you will be back. Notice how rest feels when it is named plainly instead of snatched in secret.

exercises.title: Give someone your best half hour
exercises.sub: Before opening messages, pick one task that directly helps a specific person today. Write down who it helps and how, then spend thirty focused minutes on it. You will know it helped if you finish something useful for them without starting the day scattered.

exercises.title: Try a written update
exercises.sub: Pick your next recurring status meeting. Offer to replace it with a short written update, or close the call with named next steps and clear owners. It paid off if you get calendar time back or leave knowing exactly who does what next.

exercises.title: Try an 80/20 day
exercises.sub: Use 80/20 as a loose reflection. Give the open time you have to something you value, and leave room to unwind. Care, family and rest can be the most important part of a day. Try one small change, such as trading a few minutes of scrolling for drawing. There is nothing to time or score.

exercises.title: Make room for another perspective
exercises.sub: Notice how you spend your time today, without judging it. When you find a quiet stretch, try giving 10 minutes to a science essay, a memoir, or something hands-on that interests you.

exercises.title: Name the feeling before the reach
exercises.sub: Once a day, when you catch yourself reaching for your phone, pause and name the feeling just before it: bored, anxious, lonely, avoiding. Write one word. The pattern is the lesson.

exercises.title: Guard someone else's focus
exercises.sub: Each day, protect one person's attention the way you would like yours protected. Batch your questions, wait for a natural pause, or skip the quick ping. Notice whether the quiet comes back to you.

exercises.title: Build a small example from memory
exercises.sub: Close the tutorial or guide you are following and make one small example from memory. When you stall, check the reference only to see the exact gap you missed. You will see it worked when you can redo that missing step without looking.

exercises.title: Test an old assumption
exercises.sub: Pick one inherited rule or assumption in something you control. Try a simpler version once in a small, reversible trial today. Count it a win when real results show whether to keep the change or switch back.

exercises.title: Automate one repeated step
exercises.sub: Think of something you did twice this week, like typing the same set of instructions. Make a template or shortcut and try it on one real task. Check the result yourself. Did it save time and still do the job well?

exercises.title: Close one open decision
exercises.sub: Each morning, name one small decision you have left hanging, like a reply or a purchase you keep circling. Make it, or set a date to make it. Notice what the open loop was costing you.

exercises.title: Design your own small experiment
exercises.sub: Choose one question about your own life, like "Do I think better after a walk?" Design a tiny test, run it daily, and write down what you see. You are both the scientist and the subject.

exercises.title: Offer one specific piece of help
exercises.sub: Think of one person you know who is looking for work or stuck on a task. Send a relevant job lead or one small piece of useful help with no strings attached. It worked if it saves them time or opens a door.

exercises.title: Teach one skill in two minutes
exercises.sub: Show a coworker, friend, or family member one practical shortcut or technique you can demonstrate in under two minutes. Keep it simple, then ask plainly if it actually helped them. You will know it landed when they try it themselves or tell you what clicked.

exercises.title: Listen while someone tries your work
exercises.sub: Ask one person to use something you made, like a checklist, recipe, note, or tool, while you listen quietly without explaining. Change one part where they hesitate or get stuck. You will see it helped when the next run feels smoother without you stepping in.

exercises.title: Speak up with care
exercises.sub: If someone’s contribution gets overlooked, you can name it. “That was Jo’s idea. I’d like to hear the rest.” If speaking up in the moment feels risky, check in privately and ask what would help.

exercises.title: Ask what kind of help they want
exercises.sub: When someone brings you a problem this week, first ask: "Do you want ideas, help, or just someone to hear it?" Do what they choose. Each day, notice what you wanted to do instead.

exercises.title: Pass on help you were given
exercises.sub: Recall someone who once helped you move forward. Each day, look for one small chance to give someone else that same kind of help. On day seven, consider telling your helper what it led to.

exercises.title: Would you still do it if nobody saw?
exercises.sub: Think of an online fad you’ve been tempted to try. What appeals to you about it? If you’d enjoy learning the dance even with the camera off, put on the song. If the only draw is being seen doing it, give those ten minutes to something you’ve been curious about.

exercises.title: Notice what matters
exercises.sub: What part of today will still matter a month from now? Urgent errands and alerts crowd out quieter priorities unless you make room. Give one person, task, or real break twenty undivided minutes.

exercises.title: Think for yourself
exercises.sub: It is always okay to pause and check something you heard before accepting it. Pick one claim from this week, look at what supports it, and decide for yourself whether it holds up.

exercises.title: Quietly help someone
exercises.sub: Who in your day is carrying a small load you could ease without announcing it? Clear one overlooked chore, handle a tedious job, or send an encouraging note today without looking for credit.

exercises.title: Hear another view
exercises.sub: It is easy to build your reply while someone else is still talking. You do not have to agree to hear another person clearly. In one conversation today, ask a sincere question about how they see it and listen to the end.

exercises.title: Repair one thing
exercises.sub: Everyone has moments they wish had gone better, and making things right can be gentle. Go back to one small moment, acknowledge your part honestly, and ask what would help now.

exercises.title: One small skill
exercises.sub: Name one skill you want to build and pick a small attempt for today. Afterward, record what worked and choose what to try tomorrow.

exercises.title: Notice where you shade the truth
exercises.sub: Each evening, recall one moment you bent the truth a little: to be liked, to dodge friction, to look busy. No verdict, just notice what it protected. On day seven, choose one to try differently.

exercises.title: Keep an honest evening review
exercises.sub: Before sleep, ask three quiet questions: Where was I at my best? Where did I fall short? What will I carry into tomorrow? Answer briefly and kindly. Seneca described a nightly review much like this.

exercises.title: Share one hour at a school
exercises.sub: Contact the school office or volunteer coordinator to ask what would help and whether one hour sharing a useful skill fits. Complete their screening steps, let staff manage any equipment, and respect their capacity if they are stretched.

exercises.title: Offer a library or group session
exercises.sub: Ask a local library or community group what would be useful, such as basic tech help or a short career Q&A. Follow their scheduling process, keep the format simple, and step back easily if organizers are stretched.

exercises.title: Let a neighbor choose the need
exercises.sub: Check in with a neighbor and let them choose a real need instead of guessing. Try: "Hi, I'm free Saturday from 9 to 11 if you could use a hand. Just tell me what would help, and no worries if you're busy."

exercises.title: Offer a skill with no event
exercises.sub: Offer a skill you already have to someone nearby without planning an event or spending money. Reviewing a resume, tidying a spreadsheet, or tuning a bike uses only your time. Ask what would help first, and keep it easy to decline. If your own week is full, it can wait.

exercises.title: Share something worth knowing
exercises.sub: What small detail would have saved you a second trip to the hardware store? Share the washer size that fixed your faucet, or a trick from your own week. Post it online, jot it on paper, or tell someone who could use it. There’s room for the occasional cat meme, too.

exercises.title: Learn one local name a day
exercises.sub: Each day, learn or relearn one name nearby: a neighbor, a shop clerk, someone on your usual walk. Use it once. Notice how a place changes when it has names in it.

exercises.title: Thank the people who hold it together
exercises.sub: Each day, notice one person who keeps your community running, like a crossing guard or volunteer. Thank one specifically. Midweek, ask one what quietly wears them out, and help if it fits.

exercises.title: Walk with no destination
exercises.sub: Each day, walk for five to ten minutes with no destination, podcast, or goal. Let your pace slow a little. Notice one thing you would have missed at your usual speed.

exercises.title: Name three small gifts
exercises.sub: Each evening, name three small good things from the day. A hot shower counts. Give thanks in whatever way fits you: to God, to life, to a person, or simply to the moment.

exercises.title: Sit in silence for five minutes
exercises.sub: Each day, sit for five minutes in silence. Use a prayer, a line of poetry, or your breath as a place to return when your mind wanders. Wandering is normal. Returning is the practice.

exercises.title: Listen as if it were sacred
exercises.sub: In one conversation each day, listen as if the other person were saying something precious, because to them it may be. Do not plan your reply. Notice what you hear when you are not waiting to speak.

exercises.title: Hold one question all day
exercises.sub: Each morning, choose one question to carry, like "What is asked of me today?" or "Where is love here?" Return to it a few times. At night, write one line on what the day answered, if anything.

exercises.title: Keep one daily moment of quiet
exercises.sub: Choose one ordinary moment to keep quiet on purpose: the first sip of coffee, the drive home, the dishes. Each day, enter it with a breath, a prayer, or words that mean something to you.

lessons.title: The pull before the reward
lessons.tagline: Learn to notice the reach before the thing you reach for.
lessons.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: a person waits for toast while their thumb hovers near a phone before unlocking it.

pages.title: Before the unlock
pages.body:
Your thumb moves before you have a plan.

Maybe you are standing in the kitchen waiting for toast. Maybe the elevator is taking twelve heroic seconds. Maybe you opened your laptop to do one thing, and somehow your hand has already found your phone.

That first movement is easy to miss. It happens before the app, before the feed, before the little prize or disappointment. It is the body saying, maybe there is something for me in there.

Glimmer begins here: not with the screen, but with the reach.

pages.title: Wanting is not the same as enjoying
pages.body:
There is a useful difference between wanting something and actually liking what happens after you get it.

You know this already. You can want another handful of chips and not enjoy the last few. You can want to check a message and feel worse after checking. You can want the next video, then notice your face has not moved in twenty minutes.

The wanting part is loud. It leans forward. It promises:

- relief
- novelty
- proof
- escape
- company
- a quick little spark

The liking part is quieter. It only speaks after the fact.

**Wanting says:** maybe this will help.

**Liking says:** did it?

Glimmer asks you to listen to both.

pages.title: What are you reaching for?
pages.question: What are you usually hoping will be waiting when you check?
options: 💬 A reply that changes my mood
✨ Something new enough to wake me up
🧯 Relief from a feeling I do not want to sit with
👀 Proof that I have not missed anything
🛋️ A tiny escape from the moment I am in

pages.title: The maybe hook
pages.body:
A lot of checking is powered by maybe.

Maybe there is a reply. Maybe the post took off. Maybe something happened. Maybe there is one perfect bit of news, gossip, comfort, outrage, or proof that you matter and are not floating alone in space like a sad office balloon.

The strange part is that **maybe can be stronger than yes**.

A guaranteed boring inbox is easy to ignore. An uncertain inbox keeps tapping the glass.

This does not make you foolish. It makes the moment understandable.

The work is to spot the maybe without letting it drive the car.

pages.title: The tiny handhold
pages.body:
You do not need to kill the pull. That would be a weird full-time job.

You only need one small handhold between the reach and the unlock.

Try this: when you feel the pull, silently name the promise.

- “I want relief.”
- “I want a reply.”
- “I want to stop feeling bored.”
- “I want something to happen.”

That little sentence changes the shape of the moment. The pull is still there, but now it is something you can see.

And anything you can see is not the whole of you.

pages.title: Takeaway
pages.body:
The moment before you unlock is a chance to choose how to spend the next minute.

**Try today:** When you reach for your phone out of habit, name what you hoped it would give you. Then decide whether to open it.
pages.tryToday: When you reach for your phone out of habit, name what you hoped it would give you. Then decide whether to open it.

lessons.title: The aftertaste of your inputs
lessons.tagline: Stop asking only how long it lasted. Ask how it left you.
lessons.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: a person reflects on how a digital session left them feeling.

pages.title: After you close it
pages.body:
You close the app and the room comes back.

For a second, there is a little fog. Or a little charge. Or a laugh still sitting in your chest. Or the odd hollow feeling of having eaten a whole bag of something without tasting the last half.

The timer can tell you how many minutes passed.

It cannot tell you whether those minutes fed you.

pages.title: The clock is incomplete data
pages.body:
A ten-minute check can wreck the next hour.

A forty-minute video call with someone you love can make the day feel more human.

So time matters, but it is not the whole story. If Glimmer only taught you to stare at minutes, it would miss the better clue: the aftertaste.

Aftertaste is what remains when the input is gone:

- the mood in the room
- the speed of your thoughts
- the quality of your next choice
- whether you return to your day with more of yourself, or less

That is the data worth keeping.

pages.title: Read the aftertaste
pages.question: What aftertaste do you notice most often after a digital session?
options: 🌫️ Foggy or scattered
⚡ Wired up and restless
🫥 A little empty, like nothing really landed
🤝 More connected to someone real
🌿 Settled, clearer, or genuinely restored

pages.title: Better words make better seeing
pages.body:
“Bad” is too blunt a word. So is “good.”

Try a richer menu.

A session might leave you:

- soothed
- sparked
- connected
- informed
- jealous
- wound up
- flattened
- avoidant
- amused
- hurried
- lonely
- steadier
- vaguely coated in internet dust

The more specific the word, the less you have to moralize. “I am a mess” becomes “that left me agitated.” That is not a verdict. It is usable information.

This is the whole spirit of Glimmer: notice the result without turning yourself into the problem.

pages.title: The next-choice test
pages.body:
Here is a simple way to read aftertaste:

**Look at what the session makes easier next.**

After reading a thoughtful article, it might be easier to sit down and write.

After twenty minutes of outrage, it might be easier to keep hunting for more outrage.

After messaging a friend, it might be easier to do the dishes because the world feels less cold.

The next choice tells the truth.

pages.title: Takeaway
pages.body:
Time tells you how long something lasted. Your aftertaste tells you how it left you feeling.

**Try today:** After one activity today, name the feeling it left behind in a word or two.
pages.tryToday: After one activity today, name the feeling it left behind in a word or two.

lessons.title: Quick hits and slow rewards
lessons.tagline: Learn why the easy spark can make the slower fire harder to feel.
lessons.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: quick phone sparks contrasted with slower nourishing rewards.

pages.title: The snack shelf
pages.body:
Some pleasures are like snacks on the counter.

A clip. A like. A headline. A joke.

A tiny argument you did not ask to join, but apparently your blood pressure RSVP’d yes.

They are easy to reach. They ask almost nothing from you. Often, they give you something real: a laugh, a useful tip, a moment of company.

The trouble begins when the snack shelf becomes the whole kitchen.

pages.title: Slow rewards need a runway
pages.body:
Some rewards arrive slowly:

- a walk that starts boring and ends with your shoulders lower
- a book that takes ten pages before the room gets quiet
- a conversation that warms up after the first awkward minute
- a project that feels like pushing a cart until suddenly it starts to roll

Slow rewards are not weaker. They are just easier to interrupt before they bloom.

If your attention has been trained all morning on instant sparks, the slow thing may feel broken at first. It is not broken. It is just slower than the slot-machine pace.

pages.title: Notice the trade
pages.question: What slow reward gets crowded out first when quick hits take over?
options: 📖 Reading, learning, or thinking deeply
🚶 A walk, stretch, or quiet reset
🧑‍🤝‍🧑 A real conversation I would probably enjoy
🛠️ A project that matters but starts slowly
😴 Rest that does not come with a screen in my hand

pages.title: The raised bar
pages.body:
Fast inputs can quietly raise the bar for what counts as interesting.

A paragraph has to compete with a feed designed by thousands of people you will never meet. A quiet room has to compete with breaking news, perfect dogs, strangers fighting, and someone making soup in a cabin with suspiciously good lighting.

No wonder the real world sometimes seems under-edited.

This is not a reason to hate quick hits. It is a reason to notice when they have made ordinary good things taste too plain.

pages.title: Pair the spark with a return
pages.body:
You do not need a life without quick hits. That sounds grim and a little fake.

Instead, practice returning.

Watch the funny clip, then return to the song. Check the message, then return to the paragraph. Enjoy the tiny spark, then do not let it appoint itself mayor of the next hour.

The question is not:

**“Can I avoid all fast pleasure?”**

The question is:

**“Can I still feel slower pleasure afterward?”**

pages.title: Takeaway
pages.body:
Quick pleasures and slower ones can both belong in your day. Give a slower pleasure a little time to settle in.

**Try today:** After a quick scroll, give five minutes to something you already enjoy, like a song, a sketch or a few pages. Notice how it feels.
pages.tryToday: After a quick scroll, give five minutes to something you already enjoy, like a song, a sketch or a few pages. Notice how it feels.

lessons.title: Noticing without judging
lessons.tagline: The moment gets easier to study when you stop putting yourself on trial.
lessons.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: a person observes an urge like passing weather without judging it.

pages.title: The second arrow
pages.body:
You reach for the phone.

Then you notice yourself reaching.

Then comes the extra little stab: Seriously? Again?

Now there are two things happening. First, the urge. Second, the judgment about the urge. The second one often hurts more and teaches less.

Glimmer is interested in the first moment, before the courtroom opens.

pages.title: Weather, not character
pages.body:
An urge is more like weather than a verdict.

It arrives. It changes. It may be loud. It may be inconvenient. It may ruin the picnic you thought you were having with your own attention.

But you do not have to become the weather.

Try saying:

**“Wanting is here.”**

Instead of:

**“I have no self-control.”**

The first sentence gives you a little distance. The second sentence builds a cage and hands you the key in six pieces.

Noticing is not passive. It is the first clean move.

pages.title: Catch the inner tone
pages.question: What does your inner voice usually do when you notice a habit?
options: 📋 Starts building a case against me
🙄 Says, “here we go again”
🔍 Gets curious about what led here
🧊 Goes numb and tries not to think about it
🤲 Softens a little and lets me begin again

pages.title: Curiosity beats the inner lecture
pages.body:
The inner lecture usually has terrible timing.

It shows up when you are tired, lonely, late, overstimulated, or avoiding something unpleasant. Then it acts shocked that you are not your most elegant self.

Curiosity works better.

Ask smaller, cleaner questions:

- What was happening right before the reach?
- What feeling did the phone promise to change?
- What did I need that the app could only imitate?

These are not excuses. They are clues.

And clues are much more useful than insults.

pages.title: The softer grip
pages.body:
When you stop judging the urge, you may expect it to get stronger.

Often the opposite happens.

The urge loses some of its drama because you are no longer fighting two battles. You are not obeying it, but you are not wrestling it in the mud either. You are watching, breathing, and letting the wave show you what it does.

This is not glamorous. It may look like standing in a hallway doing nothing for fifteen seconds.

That can be a real practice.

pages.title: Takeaway
pages.body:
You cannot shame yourself into clear seeing.

Judgment makes the room smoky. Noticing opens a window.

The goal is not to approve of every habit. The goal is to see clearly enough that a different choice becomes possible.

**Try today:** When an urge appears, say, “There is the reach,” and do nothing else for one breath.
pages.tryToday: When an urge appears, say, “There is the reach,” and do nothing else for one breath.

lessons.title: Attention is a muscle
lessons.tagline: The real rep is not perfect focus. It is returning.
lessons.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: a person gently returns their attention to a book or notebook.

pages.title: The paragraph you keep losing
pages.body:
You read the same paragraph three times.

On the first pass, your eyes move and your mind leaves. On the second, you get halfway through and remember a text you forgot to answer. On the third, you finally arrive inside the sentence.

It is tempting to count the first two passes as failure.

But something useful happened there: you came back.

pages.title: Returning is the rep
pages.body:
If attention is a muscle, the rep is not “never drift.”

The rep is noticing drift, then returning without making a whole opera out of it.

Back to the paragraph.

Back to the person talking.

Back to the breath, the dish, the email, the road.

**Back to the small square of life you meant to inhabit.**

Every return is small. That is why it works. You can do it again and again without needing a new personality or a sunrise routine involving seventeen jars.

pages.title: Find the return point
pages.question: When your attention wanders, what makes returning hardest?
options: 🧵 I lose the thread of what I was doing
📱 The next thing keeps pulling louder
😤 I get annoyed that I wandered at all
🪫 I am simply tired and running thin
🧩 The task is too vague to re-enter easily

pages.title: Tired attention is not bad attention
pages.body:
Muscles tire. Attention does too.

Your focus at 9 a.m. after sleep is not the same as your focus at 4:37 p.m. after messages, errands, decisions, and pretending to understand a meeting that should have been an email.

This matters because tired attention needs a kinder plan.

A kinder plan might mean:

- a shorter block
- a visible next step
- fewer open tabs
- a timer
- a pause
- a snack
- a walk around the room so your whole self remembers it has legs

You are not a machine failing to run at a constant speed.

pages.title: Training without turning life into boot camp
pages.body:
You can train attention in ordinary places.

One dish washed without a podcast.

One minute of reading before checking.

One conversation where you bring your eyes back when they drift toward the glowing rectangle nearby.

The point is not purity. The point is building trust with your own attention. You say, come back here, and slowly, over many small returns, some part of you learns the route.

pages.title: Takeaway
pages.body:
Strong attention is not attention that never leaves.

Strong attention knows the way home.

Every gentle return marks the path a little more clearly.

**Try today:** Choose one sentence, one dish, or one breath. When you wander, return once.
pages.tryToday: Choose one sentence, one dish, or one breath. When you wander, return once.

lessons.title: The hidden cost of switching
lessons.tagline: A quick check can cost more than the seconds it takes.
lessons.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: a person loses the thread of work after a quick phone check.

pages.title: The sentence disappears
pages.body:
You are writing a sentence.

A message appears. You check it, because it will only take a second.

It does take a second.

Then you return to the sentence and it has fled the scene. You can see the words you typed, but not the thread you were carrying. Now you have to rebuild the little bridge back into the work.

That rebuilding is the hidden cost.

pages.title: The check is not the whole interruption
pages.body:
The interruption has three parts:

1. **The leaving**
2. **The checking**
3. **The return**

Most people count only the middle part. “It was just ten seconds.” But the return can be the expensive part. You have to remember where you were, what mattered, what came next, and why the task did not always look this annoying.

A quick check can be quick and still costly.

pages.title: Count the real cost
pages.question: What does a “quick check” usually cost you?
options: 🧠 The thought I was holding
⏱️ More time than I expected
🌪️ A calmer mood I had just started to find
🧱 The effort of getting started again
🗣️ Presence with the person or task in front of me

pages.title: Residue
pages.body:
Some activities leave a residue:

- you read one heated comment and bring its tone into a calm email
- you check a message and keep wondering how to answer it while trying to cook dinner
- you glance at the news and your work now has a low hum underneath it

The old thing does not vanish just because the screen changed. A little of it rides along.

This is why Glimmer cares about aftertaste. Switching is not only about attention moving. It is about what attention carries with it.

pages.title: Protect the fragile parts
pages.body:
Not every moment needs protection.

Some work is sturdy. Some tasks are already chopped into pieces. Some checks are necessary, human, and worth it.

But certain moments are fragile: the first five minutes of starting, the middle of a hard paragraph, the tender part of a conversation, the calm right before sleep.

Those are the places where a “quick check” can do more damage than it admits.

You do not need to guard the whole day like a museum. Just protect the thresholds.

pages.title: Takeaway
pages.body:
The question is not:

**“Was the check short?”**

The better question is:

**“What did it interrupt?”**

A ten-second check in the wrong place can steal the thread you actually needed.

**Try today:** Before one quick check, ask: “What will I have to rebuild after this?”
pages.tryToday: Before one quick check, ask: “What will I have to rebuild after this?”

lessons.title: Boredom is a doorway
lessons.tagline: The empty moment may be where your mind starts to come back.
lessons.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: boredom as a quiet doorway into rest and imagination.

pages.title: The line at the pharmacy
pages.body:
You are waiting in line.

Nothing is happening. The person ahead of you is debating receipt options like a treaty is being drafted. Your hand starts moving toward your phone.

This is the modern reflex: any empty moment must be filled before it becomes dangerous.

But boredom is not always a problem to solve. Sometimes it is the doorway into a slower room.

pages.title: The first layer is itchy
pages.body:
The first layer of boredom is rarely peaceful.

It is itchy. It feels pointless.

It may come with a sudden need to:

- check the weather in a city you do not live in
- learn whether an actor from a show in 2009 is still married
- reorganize your entire life because the microwave has thirty seconds left

This does not mean the empty moment is useless.

It means you have reached the noisy front porch of quiet.

If you stay for a few breaths, something else may arrive: a memory, a plan, a feeling you were outrunning, a small creative thought, or simply the relief of not being fed anything for a moment.

pages.title: Stay with the gap
pages.question: What makes an empty moment hard to leave empty?
options: 🐜 It feels itchy almost immediately
📱 My hand reaches before I decide
😶 I do not want to feel what shows up
🕳️ It seems like wasted time
🤔 I am not sure what to do without input

pages.title: Filled gaps have a cost
pages.body:
A day with no empty space can look efficient from the outside.

Every line, elevator, bathroom break, red light, and couch pause gets filled. No wasted time. No awkward silence. No unmonetized eyeballs, congratulations to the shareholders.

But something is lost when every gap is plugged.

You lose the little places where:

- your mind sorts itself
- a thought finishes arriving
- a feeling finally gets noticed
- nothing grabs you for a minute

Boredom is not always rich. Sometimes it is just boring. Still, it gives attention a chance to stop sprinting.

pages.title: Stay for the second minute
pages.body:
You do not have to become a person who loves boredom. That sounds like something a suspiciously calm influencer would say near a beige wall.

Just practice staying a little longer than the first itch.

Try one tiny doorway:

- ten seconds in line
- one breath before the elevator opens
- half a minute in the parked car before the next thing begins

The doorway is small. You do not need to move in. You only need to stop slamming it shut every time it appears.

pages.title: Takeaway
pages.body:
An empty moment does not have to become a feed session. Leave a little space to notice what you want to do next. If the quiet feels uncomfortable, begin with a short pause you can manage.

**Try today:** During one wait today, keep the feed closed. Look around, stretch, or let your mind wander.
pages.tryToday: During one wait today, keep the feed closed. Look around, stretch, or let your mind wander.

lessons.title: Riding the urge wave
lessons.tagline: A brief pause can reveal how an impulse changes.
lessons.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration: a person calmly watches an urge wave crest and pass.

pages.title: The wave arrives
pages.body:
The urge does not politely knock.

It enters with its shoes on:

**Check now. Reply now. Scroll now. Buy now. Find out now.**

At the peak, it can feel like the only way out is through the habit. Not because you are weak, but because the urge is doing what waves do. It is taking up the whole view.

The useful discovery is this: waves move.

pages.title: The peak lies a little
pages.body:
At the top of an urge, your mind may make the moment sound urgent.

It may say:

- You need to know.
- You need relief.
- You need one look.
- You need to answer before the entire social fabric collapses and someone sends a search party.

Sometimes, yes, you do need to respond. Life contains actual responsibilities.

But many urges borrow the voice of an emergency. If you wait briefly, the voice often changes. It gets quieter. It becomes a request instead of a command.

That shift is worth learning from.

pages.title: Watch the crest
pages.question: What does a strong urge usually sound like in your head?
options: 🚨 “This needs to happen right now”
🧲 “Just one look and then I will stop”
🫣 “I do not want to feel this feeling”
🔄 “I need to close the loop”
🤷 “I am already doing it before I notice”

pages.title: Riding is not resisting harder
pages.body:
Riding the wave does not mean clenching your jaw and trying to become a statue.

It means staying present while the urge changes.

You might:

- put both feet on the floor
- breathe slowly
- name what is happening: “wanting is here”
- watch where the feeling rises, tightens, and starts to loosen

The goal is not to defeat the wave. The goal is to learn that you can remain yourself while it passes through.

pages.title: Decide after the crest
pages.body:
The best part of waiting is that you still get to choose.

After the crest, you may still check. That is allowed. Glimmer is not here to slap the phone out of your hand like a tiny digital crossing guard.

But checking after a pause is different from checking at the peak.

At the peak, the urge chooses for you.

After the crest, you are more likely to choose for yourself.

pages.title: Takeaway
pages.body:
An urge is not a law.

It is a moving wave with a loud beginning, a crest, and an ending you can learn to feel.

You do not have to obey the loudest second.

**Try today:** When a strong urge appears, take five slow breaths before deciding.
pages.tryToday: When a strong urge appears, take five slow breaths before deciding.

lessons.title: Why focus comes and goes
lessons.tagline: Uneven focus is a pattern you can design around, not a personal defect.
lessons.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration for Lesson 9: Why focus comes and goes.

pages.title: The real moment
pages.body: Some mornings, your attention clicks into place like a seatbelt. Other days, it slides off everything you put it on. The same person, the same life, wildly different steering.

pages.title: The useful idea
pages.body: Focus is not one switch. It is closer to weather, fuel, interest, rest, friction, and timing meeting in the same room.

pages.title: Locate yourself
pages.question: What kind of focus day is this?
options: 🔒 I can lock in if I get started
🌫️ Everything feels slippery
🎢 I swing between deep focus and total drift
🪫 I am too tired for a heroic plan
🧩 I need clearer handles

pages.title: Check the forecast first
pages.body:
Before starting one task, pause for a moment and check your real conditions: rest, fuel, noise, and interest. Skip the self-criticism and give your attention a quick forecast, like "light fog" or "steady sun."

Then match your plan to the weather. On a hazy hour, narrow the job, ask for support, or take genuine rest.

pages.title: Takeaway
pages.body:
Reading your focus like weather replaces blame with honesty, helping you scale your effort or choose rest without fighting who you are today.

**Try today:** Before one task, name today’s focus weather in two words.
pages.tryToday: Before one task, name today’s focus weather in two words.

lessons.title: Getting yourself going
lessons.tagline: Wanting to do something is not the same as crossing the starting line.
lessons.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration for Lesson 10: Getting yourself going.

pages.title: The real moment
pages.body: The file is open. The laundry is visible. The email has been aging in the corner like a cheese with opinions. You care. You really do. Still, nothing moves.

pages.title: The useful idea
pages.body: Starting often fails because the first step is secretly too large, too vague, or too emotionally loaded. The cure is not a louder inner coach. It is a smaller door.

pages.title: Locate yourself
pages.question: What blocks the first move?
options: 🧱 The task feels too big
🌫️ I cannot see the first step
😬 I am avoiding the feeling around it
📱 I keep taking easier exits
⏳ I am waiting to feel ready

pages.title: Shrink the doorway
pages.body:
Pick one task you have been circling and ask what makes the entry heavy: size, vagueness, or awkward feelings? Name that snag honestly.

Then build a smaller doorway. Instead of finishing the whole email, open the draft and write the greeting. If friction stays high, talk through the opening line with someone you trust.

pages.title: Takeaway
pages.body:
A clear first step makes starting easier.

**Try today:** Make the first step small and specific, like opening the document and writing the date.
pages.tryToday: Make the first step small and specific, like opening the document and writing the date.

lessons.title: Time blindness
lessons.tagline: If time will not feel clear from the inside, make it visible from the outside.
lessons.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration for Lesson 11: Time blindness.

pages.title: The real moment
pages.body: You look up and the afternoon has leaked out of the room. Or you think something will take ten minutes, then it quietly becomes a small historical era.

pages.title: The useful idea
pages.body: Some minds feel time as now and not-now. A timer, clock, calendar block, or visible cue gives time a shape you do not have to invent by force.

pages.title: Locate yourself
pages.question: Where does time disappear?
options: 🕳️ Scrolling or video loops
🧹 Chores that expand forever
💬 Messages and replies
🛠️ Projects with no clear edge
🚪 Transitions between things

pages.title: Give time an outside edge
pages.body:
Give one slippery activity, like answering messages, tidying, or browsing, an outside marker before you begin. Choose a cue you will actually register: a desk clock, a soft chime, a vibrating watch, or two favorite songs.

When the marker finishes, check in and decide clearly whether to continue, switch gears, or pause.

pages.title: Takeaway
pages.body:
Relying on an outside cue is not a flaw. It simply gives passing time a shape you can sense before an hour quietly slips away.

**Try today:** Set one visible timer before starting a slippery activity.
pages.tryToday: Set one visible timer before starting a slippery activity.

lessons.title: A mind that runs on interest
lessons.tagline: Interest is not a luxury. Sometimes it is the handle that lets you move.
lessons.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration for Lesson 12: A mind that runs on interest.

pages.title: The real moment
pages.body: A boring task can sit in front of you like cold toast. Important, yes. Inspiring, absolutely not. The trick is not to pretend it sparkles. The trick is to borrow a little spark.

pages.title: The useful idea
pages.body: Novelty, challenge, company, a deadline, music, a race against a timer, or a stranger pen can make a dull task grippable. This is design, not cheating.

pages.title: Locate yourself
pages.question: What kind of interest helps you start?
options: 🎲 Novelty or a fresh angle
⏱️ A short timer or deadline
🤝 Someone nearby
🏁 A tiny challenge
🎧 A mood-setting sound or ritual

pages.title: Pair flat work with spark
pages.body:
Take one flat, necessary chore, like folding laundry, sorting bills, or updating a form, and pair it with something mildly engaging. Queue a favorite album or podcast, switch to a brighter pen, sit somewhere fresh, or turn ten minutes into a playful race.

You do not have to pretend the task is thrilling to give your mind a handle.

pages.title: Takeaway
pages.body:
Adding warmth, novelty, or rhythm to boring work is smart design, not cheating, because attention moves better when it has something real to grip.

**Try today:** Add one small source of interest to a dull task.
pages.tryToday: Add one small source of interest to a dull task.

lessons.title: The hardest part is starting
lessons.tagline: A silly-small start is often wiser than a serious plan.
lessons.heroAlt: Cartoon illustration for Lesson 13: The hardest part is starting.

pages.title: The real moment
pages.body: “Clean the kitchen” sounds like a government program. “Put one cup in the sink” sounds like a thing a human can do before the kettle boils.

pages.title: The useful idea
